title: Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza
description: Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents where displaced residents have been living in Gaza, with a United Nations official saying almost e
body: Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents where displaced residents have been living in Gaza, with a United Nations official saying almost everyone in the territory needs help.Residents used pots and pans to clear water from their flooded tents, with some saying they were left without shelter.Jonathan Veitch, the Unicef representative for Palestine, said the "desperate" situation was being made worse by Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and supplies such as engine oil.Some 90% of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas, many of them multiple times, with limited access to clean water and sanitation.Aid agencies say the situation is likely to worsen with the start of the rainy season.Speaking to the BBC from Deir Al Balah in central Gaza, Veitch said: "It's just horrific and they're absolutely desperate. "We're providing all the assistance that we can but we're getting stopped on the street as we're driving now because people are begging us for help."The Hamas-run government in Gaza said about 70,000 tents had been flooded. A spokesperson said the "collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs" had caused injuries, some of which were critical.Veitch also said there were fewer tarpaulins, plastic sheeting and tents available in the Gaza strip due to UN budget cuts."We have to be much more choosy about where we're going to be supporting," he said. "But unfortunately, heavy flooding this morning means that nearly everyone needs help."Israel has said it restricts the entry of items into Gaza that could be used for military purposes.Maryam Odeh, 34, who lives with her children in Deir al-Balah, told AFP news agency: "We no longer know how to protect our children. "My children ask me where we will sleep tonight, and I have no answer."Khaled al-Najjar, 41, told AFP: "We fear for our children not only from the flooding of the tents, but also from the cold and the widespread diseases."Veitch said aid workers were being "stopped on the street" by Gazans "begging us for help".He continued: "They're absolutely desperate. We saw last year what winter does, and we had deaths from hypothermia last year. "We can expect the same again unless we have very, very urgent action now."A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war.The conflict was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.

schema.headline: Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza

title: Dolly Parton's manager drops lawsuit against her nephew
description: The manager of the late country music star Dolly Parton has dropped a lawsuit against her nephew.The civil case was filed by the company that manages
body: The manager of the late country music star Dolly Parton has dropped a lawsuit against her nephew.The civil case was filed by the company that manages Parton's business interests less than a month after her death.It included allegations of threats, intimidation and coercion against Bryan Seaver, the relative who publicly confirmed Parton had died in August. A temporary restraining order was also sought.Seaver, who previously served as Parton's head of security, denied the allegations.In a statement to the BBC's US partner, CBS News, Seaver's attorneys said he was "grateful to put this misunderstanding behind him so that the family can grieve peacefully".Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns the security firm Squadron Augmented Protection Services (SAPS).It provided security to Parton, who died of cancer aged 80, for the final 20 years of her life.Weeks after Seaver confirmed her death, both he and his company were dismissed by She's Alive, which manages Parton's estate.Danny Nozell, Parton's longtime manager and the head of She's Alive, filed for a temporary restraining order against Seaver and his company, which was granted by a judge.In court filings, he accused Seaver of "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", after demanding payment from the estate. The documents included messages in which he allegedly threatened to damage Parton's brand and business interests if his demands were not met.The filings also alleged that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees. Seaver denied threatening the estate and in a statement published by TMZ at the time, he said he was a "career soldier and military contractor" but insisted he had simply been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".

schema.headline: Dolly Parton's manager drops lawsuit against her nephew

title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, says Barnier
description: The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy B
body: The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago.But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access.He said there was not a "single market à la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt.Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms"."There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market."Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit.Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime. Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum.Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll.Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point.He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship.Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member.The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises."Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. It was a lie".The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent £350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead". Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly £350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS". Critics have said that the £350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's £75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK.Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the £350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise. ​In his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only £175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money".Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the £350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth."

schema.headline: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, says Barnier

title: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
description: Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and dis
body: Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow."The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said."In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering."The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States. He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin."The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

schema.headline: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes

title: Monty Don bids 'final goodbye' to Gardeners' World after two decades
description: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Monty Done! Monty and his dog, Ned, have been a fixture on the showByPaul GlynnCulture reporterTV hortic
body: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Monty Done! Monty and his dog, Ned, have been a fixture on the showByPaul GlynnCulture reporterTV horticulturalist Monty Don thanked viewers and his furry friend Ned the dog while presenting his final episode of Gardeners' World, after more than two decades on air.The head gardener on the long-running BBC TV series signed off from Longmeadow garden, where the show has been based for 16 years, on Friday."From myself, Ned, and Longmeadow it's the final goodbye," he said on the programme, adding it had been "a privilege and pleasure" to share his garden experiences with so many people.During the episode, Don, 71, confirmed he would remain part of the presenting line-up for next year's Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) Chelsea Flower Show.Image caption, Monty Don started on Gardeners' World in 2003, replacing Alan TitchmarshHe added he will feature in two winter specials, expected to air between now and Christmas.One celebratory episode will see him reflect on his years presenting the series and the changes he has seen at Longmeadow, external, which is also the garden of his private home, which he and his wife Sarah bought in 1991.'Good luck with your own gardens'Don replaced Alan Titchmarsh on the show in 2003, at his predecessor's request."I first began presenting Gardeners' World 23 years ago at Berryfields, and we came here to Longmeadow 16 years ago - in that time, things have changed," he recalled, on Friday's farewell."The garden has grown, Nigel has been and gone, and Nellie and Patty [his previous dogs], but there has been one constant factor, and that has been the incredible privilege and pleasure of sharing my garden and my gardening life with you here, as well as working with so many superb people."So, thank you. Thank you for coming on that journey with me and good luck with your own gardens in the future. So, for the last time... goodbye."Image source, BBC StudiosDetails of the next series of Gardeners' World will be announced at a later date, the BBC noted in a statement ahead of Don's farewell. His successor has not yet been named. Bookmakers and viewers have pointed to regular co-presenters like Frances Tophill and Adam Frost as top contenders, though Tophill has played down expectations of stepping directly into his shoes.Prior to fronting Gardeners' World, Don hosted other shows including Tomorrow's World, Holiday and - a preview of coming attractions - a gardening segment on This Morning.He took a three-year break from the programme after suffering a minor stroke in 2008.In September this year, Don announced that the current series would be his last. In a statement, he said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience", but added that "now is the right time for a change".The BBC said at the time that Don had "inspired and guided millions of viewers with his warmth, wisdom and passion for gardening" since joining the programme in 2003.Don was made an OBE by Queen Elizabeth, in 2018, for services to horticulture, broadcasting and charity. And he also received the RHS Victoria Medal of Honour - highest honour in horticulture.His final episode of Gardeners' World is available to stream now on BBC iPlayer.

schema.headline: Monty Don bids 'final goodbye' to Gardeners' World after two decades

title: Married at First Sight UK: Relief, tears and sadness - how cast reacted to Channel 4 show being axed
description: Figure caption, Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegationsByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentUpdated 5 hours ago"I'm delighted and so re
body: Figure caption, Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegationsByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentUpdated 5 hours ago"I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else will have to go through the same again."That's what one woman - who alleged she was raped on Married at First Sight UK - texted to me, as the news broke that the show was being cancelled.Another woman, who also says her on-screen husband raped her, was in tears at the news. She told us she felt "great, consuming relief", but added she was "astounded" it had taken an external review for Channel 4 to finally pull the plug on the show.Commenting on the review, she said: "Suggesting the programme could reasonably continue with the implementation of a 'safe word', 'panic button' or 'lockable bathroom with an extra bolt inside' is absolute insanity to me."The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis in May this year, after BBC Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.As the news emerged on Thursday morning that Married at First Sight UK - better known as MAFS UK - was being axed, my colleagues and I reached out to the three women who had contributed to our investigation.None of them had been informed in advance of the decision to cancel the show, they said, although two had contributed to the review.Image source, Married at First Sight UK, CPL ProductionsImage caption, Shona Manderson appeared on the 2023 series of Married at First Sight UKShona Manderson told me by telephone her main feeling was relief that their voices had been heard."Speaking out wasn't easy, but knowing that our voices have helped bring about change makes it all worthwhile," she said.Over the day, more MAFS UK cast members were in touch with us.Several were pleased by the decision to scrap the series, but others said it did not go far enough and called for more accountability.One cast member, who asked to remain anonymous, said people watching at home do not always appreciate this "isn't simply a television show" for those taking part."These are real people, real emotions."Image source, Jeff Spicer/Getty Images for SXSW LondonImage caption, April Banbury took part in the 2022 series of MAFS UKOthers we spoke to felt the show should have been taken off-air sooner.They include April Banbury, who took part in the 2022 series and whose on-screen husband was subsequently arrested on suspicion of controlling and coercive behaviour. The police investigation against him was later dropped, and her partner called the allegations against him "false"."I'm glad MAFS has been cancelled. It should have happened years ago," Banbury told us. "We want answers, we want those responsible to be held accountable, and we want to know how this was allowed to happen in the first place,” added another cast member, who asked to remain anonymous. He was echoed by Lia Perin, Partner at Taylor Hampton and lawyer for a number of MAFS UK participants.“Cancelling the show may prevent future harm, but it does not resolve questions about the treatment of previous contestants,” she told the BBC."Channel 4 owes them answers, not simply assurances that lessons have been learned."Image source, Lara EyreImage caption, Lara Eyre was a bride on the 2022 seriesOthers writing on social media said their experiences had been more positive, and that they were sad to see it go.Jay Howard, from the 2023 series, external, said the show had brought her friendships and opportunities, while Marilyse Corrigan, a 2021 bride, external, said it was a chapter of her life she looked back on "with fond memories".A number of cast members we spoke to also expressed concern for staff who had been working on the show, as well as sorrow for fans.Lara Eyre, who appeared on the 2022 series, told me she felt we were now "on the edge of a curb on how we treat reality TV stars and safeguarding", adding it was a "real shame" for those who filmed this year's series, which will never be aired, as well as a shame for fans of the show."I know a lot of people loved it, I loved it," she said.“Yes, I know it was traumatic, for sure, and there was a lot of bad things that went with the good. But it was a big part of a lot of people's lives, so it's sad it's not going to be on any more, but I also think this could've been avoided."Where does this go from here?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Channel 4's office in central LondonAs the dust settles, there are still many questions. Only "a summary of findings" from Channel 4’s review has been released, rather than the full report.We still do not know what the broadcaster did when it was first warned about the serious allegations by the production company.Why did it take them so long to investigate? And why did they only do so once BBC Panorama raised the alarm?We put some of these questions to Channel 4's boss Priya Dogra on Thursday. She said the broadcaster's handling of incidents as they arose was appropriate, and that the review had borne that out.In a statement to BBC News on Friday, Channel 4 said its review “did not seek to adjudicate on the serious allegations of wrongdoing against a small number of past contributors highlighted by Panorama, as those allegations remain a matter for the relevant authorities”.The Dark Side of Married at First SightPanorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.Watch on iPlayer nowIt said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom’s broadcasting code.Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee on 17 November, so we may hear more then.Either way, this is not the end of the story. There is an ongoing Ofcom investigation into the show - and in June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.The decision to scrap MAFS UK will also inevitably raise questions about what happens with the wider Married at First Sight format.If one broadcaster says the show has “run its course,” then those global versions may also come under the spotlight.Channel 4 has already said it will not be showing international editions like MAFS Australia again.And for the TV industry more broadly, questions will once again be asked about reality TV - and whether shows like this can ever keep their contributors safe.If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.ukGet in touchWhat is your reaction to the cancellation of MAFS UK? Get in touch.

schema.headline: Married at First Sight UK: Relief, tears and sadness - how cast reacted to Channel 4 show being axed

title: Victims in rape cases must not feel like they are on trial, Burnham says
description: Andy Burnham has said the government needs to make sure that victims in rape cases do not feel like they are on trial.His comments come after Metropol
body: Andy Burnham has said the government needs to make sure that victims in rape cases do not feel like they are on trial.His comments come after Metropolitan Police boss Sir Mark Rowley told the BBC that what he heard reported from Russell Brand's trial came very close to "victim blaming".The government needs to "constantly look" at how rape trials are conducted to better support alleged victims in court, the prime minister told Times Radio, although BBC News understands there are no plans to change the law around rape trials. Actor and comedian Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault after a four-week trial in London.  During an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, it was put to Sir Mark that Brand's defence barrister Ian Winter KC "told jurors none of the complainants had in his words 'resisted, screamed or even tried to leave'".Sir Mark replied: "I think what I've heard reported heads towards, it's getting very close to victim blaming, which is something we've thought very hard about in policing and make sure we don't do."He said he would support a call from the Victims' Commissioner for a legal duty that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial."It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case," Sir Mark explained. In a Times Radio interview on Saturday, Burnham said he would "look closely" at the police chief's comments.He said the government needed to look at how to "make sure they do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court"."[I'm] always prepared to make changes," he said. "We need to encourage more women to come forward to report rape, we need to get the conviction rate up. "All of this is part of our broader agenda as a government combatting violence against women and girls." Pressed on whether this might lead to a change in the law, the prime minister replied: "I wouldn't rule anything out... I will study what's happened here in great detail."Brand, who has starred in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall, will be sentenced on Monday and is expected to face substantial jail time.He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault after the jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours.The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody.It has since been revealed that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Met said its investigation "remains ongoing".Sir Mark told BBC Breakfast he "wouldn't be surprised if many more came forward".In the wake of Brand's trial, Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman said rape trials must be conducted "in a way that challenges myths and misconceptions about sexual violence". In a social media post, Waxman wrote that "victims need confidence that the justice process is fair and based on evidence, not myths and false assumptions about rape and trauma". Speaking to the Today programme on Saturday, director and founder of the Centre for Women's Justice Harriet Wistrich agreed that juries need to understand "underlying behaviours" without "running to judgement" over how a victim behaved in a particular way.But former Conservative MP Anna Soubry, who has now returned to her work as a barrister where she often defends rape and sexual offence cases in the Crown court, told the BBC "people are being misled" by Sir Mark's comments."Every single judge in those cases must give, and does give, a very firm direction to the jury on exactly these points," she said.As a result, she said she was " really disappointed" in the police chief and stressed "we've got to trust our juries" who are able to have an understanding of the nature of sexual offences.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

schema.headline: Victims in rape cases must not feel like they are on trial, Burnham says

title: Baxters fish soup cans recalled over fears they could 'swell and rupture'
description: Customers who bought cans of a fish soup manufactured by Baxters have been urged to dispose of them in outside bins over fears the tins could burst.Th
body: Customers who bought cans of a fish soup manufactured by Baxters have been urged to dispose of them in outside bins over fears the tins could burst.The firm has recalled its Chef Selections Cullen Skink soup, a smoked haddock chowder, due to a manufacturing fault which may cause it to spoil and cans to "swell and potentially rupture", according to the Food Standards Agency (FSA)., externalIf spoilt, the soup may have an "unpleasant odour and flavour", the FSA said.The company, based in the north east of Scotland, said the issue may affect the 400g cans with batch code L07XC and an April 2029 best before date. Shoppers who bought the soup in England, Wales and Scotland have been told not to eat it, and to instead dispose of it without opening it."Carefully place the full can in a bag and dispose of it in an external bin," the FSA told customers.People seeking a replacement are told to contact Baxters customer care team at ccuk@baxters.com.Founded in Fochabers in Moray in 1868, Baxters remains one of Scotland's best-known food manufacturers. It remains a privately-owned family business and is now run by fourth-generation family member Audrey Baxter.

schema.headline: Baxters fish soup cans recalled over fears they could 'swell and rupture'

title: New Zealand election: No clear winner after tight general election
description: Figure caption, New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?ByOlivia Ireland and Tiffanie TurnbullReporting fromWellingtonUpdated 1 hour a
body: Figure caption, New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?ByOlivia Ireland and Tiffanie TurnbullReporting fromWellingtonUpdated 1 hour agoThere was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.Image source, EPAImage caption, New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon addressed supporters in Auckland as votes were being countedThe electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground". More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share. But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern". "It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points. Image source, ReutersImage caption, Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins speaking to supportersJulian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

schema.headline: New Zealand election: No clear winner after tight general election

title: Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says 'cyber-criminals' shared his personal data on dark web
description: Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says he has been targeted by "cyber-criminals" who published his personal data online because of his country's
body: Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says he has been targeted by "cyber-criminals" who published his personal data online because of his country's support for Ukraine."For days now, cyber-criminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation," Tajani wrote on X.He did not specify the nature of the threats, but said the hackers were also targeting his family.The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that is not indexed by common search engines and can only be accessed with specialist software."Our position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted," Tajani said."Defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation's democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities."Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed the incident on pro-Russian hackers and offered Tajani her "full solidarity"."The sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a cause of serious concern and must be tackled with the utmost determination," she said in a statement.Moscow has not publicly responded to the allegations.Meloni also expressed concern about "circulation of false images" which she said were shared by members of Italy's opposition. She did not give details about the content of the images.The Italian government has provided humanitarian and military support to Ukraine in its war against Russia.Tajani, who is also the deputy prime minister, said the government was taking the threats seriously.

title: What happens if the internet goes down? BlackSky - the UK's emergency backup plans
description: It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong."I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everythin
body: It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong."I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everything went off," the professor at Lancaster University told the BBC. "Streetlights were off. The sodium glow that we can see over the horizon from Morecambe was off." The next day he went for a walk."[It was] almost like a zombie movie," he said. "People trying to find phone reception, wondering where things were, and there was a huge queue at the one working telephone box."At 22:45 on 5 December 2015, the River Lune - which flows directly through Lancaster - had flooded, and the electricity supply to 61,500 people in the city went.Households lost light and heat, some water supplies also began to fail because they relied on electric pumps. The railway station closed. So too petrol stations and shops. Most cash machines didn't work. Traffic lights failed.The two communication systems that survived were copper wire landline telephones and FM radio. The local commercial radio station The Bay had an emergency generator and one landline and a reporter was sent outside the affected area to ring in with information.Three months later, Kemp, a professor of engineering with a specialism in safety and electrical systems, gathered people together to look at everything that had gone wrong."It is perhaps ironic that, in a society with huge commitment to digital infrastructure, the most reliable source of news was a commercial station using technology that would have been familiar to the engineers on the 1960s Radio Caroline pirate radio ship," the subsequent report concluded. For Kemp and others in the field of civil contingency, Lancaster was a warning. When a town loses power for several days, our connected world falls apart. This kind of disruption has been given a name: a Black Sky event. At a recent summit on UK resilience, the conversation focused on the need for the UK to be able to withstand a Black Sky event for a minimum of 72 hours. "We are nine meals from anarchy" is a phrase often heard in the civil contingency world. A brutal reminder of the fear that three days without food would be enough to turn a crisis into chaos. If a Black Sky event takes out electricity, water, shops and communications, there is a good reason the government wants us to have our own supplies.The much talked about "Be Ready" campaign is designed to help ready us for all sorts of possible crises, but the government says there is no specific threat to the grid. Regardless, a Black Sky event is definitely at the backs of people's minds.In a major emergency, we are being told to hunker down and turn on an FM radio, as thousands did in Lancaster. This is why the BBC has its own Black Sky plan. Only a small number of staff know the full details, but from what I have gleaned, about 100 people in the BBC will run a special emergency radio studio. It will have secure lines of communication not dependent on the internet, and fuel, water and food to ensure it can operate without resupply for at least three days.This emergency service will broadcast pre-arranged government messaging. The scripts have already been published online., external They include instructions on how much people should be drinking each day and how to dispose of toilet waste without flushing the toilet.Other information will be broadcast via satellite vehicles from a select number of journalists at emergency centres around the UK, which will carry on as long as the diesel lasts.The BBC's broadcasts will be sent via radio transmission towers, isolated from the internet and equipped with tanks of between five and 40,000 litres (8,800 gallons) of diesel to keep their generators going for three days - FM radio is power hungry. The teams will be using satellite phones to keep in touch and if these stop working there are pre-agreed protocols and meet-up points.Why FM? Because it works almost everywhere, even in a blackout or a crippling cyber-attack."It was originally thought we should plan for five to seven days," I was told quietly by one BBC insider. "The latest advice from Neso [National Energy System Operator] is that they will probably be able to get the power back on in two to three days."Of course, fears of a grid failure are not new, but recent events such as the mass blackout in Spain, Portugal and south-western France in April 2025 have pushed it up the agenda. And the more it happens, the more it reveals the problems it can create in our networked world.People need to know power cuts are about more than just the lights going out, says Lord Harris, chair of the UK's National Preparedness Commission. ''It's likely to stop the water supply because unless you happen to be located neatly downstream of a reservoir, that requires electricity," he told me.More importantly, sewage tends to solidify unless water can move through it, he adds, "and that then causes blockages, the whole thing backs up, you get sewage flowing out, flowing back up the system".It's common for governments in Europe to regularly advise households to stock up on supplies in case of a national emergency - but the UK is behind in its warnings to the population. However, work has begun on some backup systems, such as High Altitude Pseudo-Satellites (HAPS). The government is spending £70m developing planes that can circle over the UK and provide at least a week of emergency mobile phone and internet connectivity at times of crisis. "When ground networks fail, there are limits to what satellites can provide as a fallback," said Rico Chandra, programme director for Enduring Atmospheric Platforms, the company developing HAPS plans.  We live in a complex, electrically powered world - but the more connected everything becomes the more catastrophic it is when that fails. In the drive towards efficiency over the last five decades, we've lost backup systems, says Lord Harris.An example of this is the new communication system being adopted by the emergency services, which will replace radio comms with mobile phone network technology, says Lord Harris, "so if the mobile phone goes down it will also impact on emergency services communications". However, the government insists "moving emergency services onto modern 4G and 5G technologies" is "resilient and reliable".The Cabinet Office said: "The UK has one of the most resilient electricity systems in the world, and there has never been a complete outage in the grid's 75-year history."Government enthusiasm for resilience is nothing new. Oliver Dowden, the then deputy prime minister, launched the last Conservative government's disaster planning initiative in May 2024. The launch was somewhat overshadowed by Sunak announcing an election on the same day but, two years on, calls for at least three days of resilience have only grown stronger.At the beginning of researching this article I spoke to an engineer about the UK's TV and radio transmission masts, their lonely isolation from the rest of the digital landscape sounded like a failing. It now feels like an argument in their favour. The current urgency for disaster planning is coming at an interesting moment for technology we used to rely on. The UK's copper wire landline system - which would work even in a power cut - will be switched off on 31 January 2027. The future of FM radio is also under government review.The response from the government was that while  copper landlines had been a useful fallback during power cuts, they were now unreliable and difficult to repair.As I ended my call with Kemp, I asked him if his report had helped improve our readiness for a Black Sky. He paused."If anything, we've gone backwards," he said. "Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you've no longer got power."While writing this piece last Saturday I had to break off for an hour because my street was suddenly plunged into darkness. We had a power cut.I found my emergency torch, but the batteries had leaked. My candles had been pushed to the back of a cupboard and I had no idea where I had put my wind-up radio with its emergency torch.It felt like an omen.

title: Three held after boy hurt in sword attack near Gloucester school
description: Two men arrested after boy injured in sword attackImage source, PAImage caption, Police attended St Peter's High School in Tuffley, Gloucester, at 08:
body: Two men arrested after boy injured in sword attackImage source, PAImage caption, Police attended St Peter's High School in Tuffley, Gloucester, at 08:50 GMT on FridayByKirsten RobertsonWest of EnglandUpdated 2 hours agoTwo men and a boy have been arrested after a teenager was injured in an attack involving a sword near two schools in Gloucester.St Peter's High School and Willow Primary Academy, in Tuffley, were put into lockdown after the incident at 08:50 GMT on Friday. Police said a 17-year-old suffered a wound "believed to have been caused by the sword". A 19-year-old was arrested overnight on suspicion of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. An 18-year-old was held on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. Meanwhile another 17-year-old boy was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.The trio - who are all from Gloucester - remain in police custody for questioning.Two men, one with a sword, had been seen chasing two boys, according to police on Friday.Armed officers attended the scene to search for the suspects who reportedly fled on foot.Police said the 17-year-old suffered a "superficial wound believed to have been caused by the sword". The other boy involved was not injured.Image caption, The incident happened close to two Gloucester schoolsGloucestershire Police also said a woman who had previously been arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender had been released on police bail.At the school gates outside St Peter's High School on Friday, a pupil called Jimmy told the BBC the situation was "really scary" and that they had been told to lock doors and turn lights off."At the time I was scared. My heart was racing," he said.Jimmy said pupils were locked in their classrooms for several hours.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Gloucestershire

title: Sao Paulo Grand Prix: Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to have grid penalties
description: Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc will all have grid penalties at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.Verstappen w
body: Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc will all have grid penalties at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.Verstappen will start from the back of the grid while Hamilton and Leclerc will both have 10-place penalties.They join Mercedes driver George Russell in having penalties for using too many engine parts. Russell's drop is only five places.Verstappen will have an an all-new engine fitted after Red Bull discovered problems after Friday practice.Leclerc, Hamilton and Russell have all fitted new internal combustion engines.The penalties for the Ferrari drivers are bigger than Russell's because it is the first time they have exceeded the limit of four engines per season, while Russell had already gone beyond that.Verstappen famously won the 2024 Sao Paulo Grand Prix from 17th on the grid after an engine penalty in a wet race.

schema.headline: Sao Paulo Grand Prix: Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to have grid penalties

title: Buildings evacuated in Liverpool city centre after car crash causes gas leak
description: A gas leak caused by a car crashing into a restaurant in Liverpool city centre has led to road closures and the evacuation of neighbouring buildings.T
body: A gas leak caused by a car crashing into a restaurant in Liverpool city centre has led to road closures and the evacuation of neighbouring buildings.The incident happened at about 12:30 GMT on North John Street when a Peugeot car hit the window of Tiger Rock Restaurant, Merseyside Police said.The driver stayed at the scene and there is no indication that this was a deliberate act, the force said.Three people who had been in the restaurant at the time of the crash were assessed for minor injuries, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said.A spokesman said the impact caused a gas leak so a cordon has been put in place by firefighters and the police, with a structural engineer and a gas engineer due to attend.Neighbouring buildings have been evacuated as a precaution and road closures are in place at the junction of Dale Street and North John Street, and also the junction of North John Street and Lord Street.Buses have also been temporarily diverted with all Wirral Metro services terminating at Whitechapel, and starting their return journey from Sir Thomas Street.

schema.headline: Buildings evacuated in Liverpool city centre after car crash causes gas leak
